newsitem.title: UK: When Davis dons raincoat, commodities traders panic.
newsitem.headline: When Davis dons raincoat, commodities traders panic.

text.p: Jon Davis remembers walking through the trading room at Shearson Lehman Hutton in Chicago in June 1988 on his way outside to buy a bagel and coffee for breakfast.
The traders immediately panicked because Davis, Shearson's meteorologist, was wearing a trenchcoat.
They assumed he was expecting rain when the farm-rich Midwest was entering a severe drought that had sent prices of agricultural commodities soaring.
"The market was so sensitive that anything got people into an uproar," said Davis, now the meteorologist at Smith Barney.

The reaction provoked by his wardrobe hammered home to Davis how big a role the weather plays in volatile commodities markets, where millions of dollars are traded every day in oil, cotton, gold, sugar and pork bellies, to name just a few.

He used to spend about 90 percent of his time on forecasts that affect the grains and soybeans markets, but now half his day is devoted to energy markets where cold temperatures or hurricanes can upset the supply-demand balance.

Explosive growth in energy futures trading, deregulation in the U.S. and European gas and electricity industries, and tight home heating oil supplies this year have been a boon for meteorologists' services.

Oil prices this year hit their highest levels since the 1991 Gulf War and the industry is demanding more sophisticated and thorough weather forecasts to guard against energy shortages after a particularly cold winter last year.
In the last 10 years high-powered satellites and supercomputers that calculate data into weather formulas have stretched the reliability of forecasts from three to five days to 10 to 14.

The forecasts are derived from government calculations that incorporate data from all over the world. Water buoys are placed in the ocean and balloons sent as high as 80,000 to 90,000 feet to calculate temperature, humidity and winds.
But science is just one factor going into weather forecasts, meteorolgists say.
"Every meteorologist has the same general information to look at ... but how you use it is different and that is how art comes into it," said Davis.

His words are echoed by Michael Palmerino, a senior meteorologist at Weather Services Corp. in Lexington, Mass., where 80 to 90 meteorologists work around the clock to advise trading and media clients.
"There is usually an understanding between the client and the meteorologist that this is far from an exact science," Palmerino said.
Weather forecasting has also entered cyberspace. Weather Services Corp. is one of a host of weather services offering their forecasts on the Internet.

The privatisation and restructuring of the British gas industry, for example, has spawned the need for daily site-specific forecasts, used to estimate regional and national demand and the deployment of maintenance staff.

"We look at the past 2-3 years of data from a company and look at the weather, and then make a formula and use the weather to predict what future sales will be," said Stewart Wass, manager of consulting and planning group in Bracknell, England.

A one degree Celsius change in temperature in Britain, for example, results in a 1 percent change in electricity demand, with heavy rainfall creating a 2 percent change, strong winds a 10-20 percent shift and clouds a 25 percent increase, he said.
Merrill Lynch brokers and traders receive two complete weather reports a day, as well as twice-daily conference calls with a meteorologist from ACCUweather.
"We tend to downplay the validity of any forecast beyond 10 days," said William O'Neill, director of futures research in New York.
But he said the weather was "particularly important this year because of the very low level of distillate (including heating oil) stocks."
Oil brokers and analysts in Europe said they talk to their colleagues in Moscow and the United States to hear first hand what the weather is like.

Traders track hurricanes brewing in the Caribbean that might hit refineries and shipping paths, storms in the North Sea that could cut crude production, and cold weather in the northeast United States and Germany, two key heating oil regions.

They also demand information on the Russian Black Sea ports and the Baltic and Mediterranean for delays in tanker loadings and freezing conditions on the river Rhine where barges transport refined products.
